failure_modes: Co-isolated non-vesicular particles (lipoproteins, protein aggregates, or other secretome components) that carry or bind the same antigenic epitopes co-fractionate with particle peaks and produce capture-positive signal, producing false-positive identity assignment despite MISEV-recommended orthogonal assays.

Detergent + protease/RNase sensitivity of capture signal reflects selective loss or disruption of fragile particle subpopulations or assay interference (capture-reagent incompatibility with buffer or detergent) rather than definitive evidence of bona fide membrane protection, producing misleading interpretation of membrane-associated display.

Assay sensitivity and dynamic range are insufficient in low-biomass or scale-relevant fractions, causing false negatives (failure-to-detect bona fide EV surface phenotype) that could block manufacturable candidates or produce inconsistent lot-to-lot pass/fail calls.

Buffer- or reagent-incompatibility with capture antibodies/TIM4/AnxA5 (or with particle-count instrumentation) generates artifactual signal loss or spurious signal, confounding detergent-protection interpretations and reducing reproducibility across runs.

Reproducibility failure across independent conditioned-medium lots (biological variability of MSC source cells, passage, or processing) leads to inconsistent identity gating and undermines comparability workflows.

Adopting the identity gate prior to demonstrating manufacturable yields or linkage to recoverable in vivo exposure imposes process constraints that are not feasible at scale, causing programmatic delays or inappropriate process changes.

Interpreting a positive intact-surface-phenotype readout as evidence of likely in vivo delivery (a potency/PK surrogate) without direct in vivo verification leads to misprioritization of candidates that will fail biodistribution or efficacy testing.
strongest_objection: Even if the proposed orthogonal capture + detergent/protease-protection workflow reproducibly identifies a membrane-protected, capture-positive particle population in vitro, that identity metric may not meaningfully predict recoverable in vivo exposure or delivery after intranasal dosing — so using it as a product-identity gate risks giving a false assurance that the material is a therapeutically relevant EV preparation. Non-human-primate intranasal biodistribution data showing strong nasal retention and negligible brain uptake highlight that intact-EV surface-phenotype measurements in manufacturing/fractionation may be disconnected from the dominant delivery barriers and species-dependent biodistribution, and thus could mislead decisions about advancement or comparability without direct short-interval in vivo validation.
